column6: Core Idea said the bounds prove "asymptotic density 1/ln(x)", which is the PNT and contradicts the new misconception bullet; changed to "density of order 1/ln(x)". Also noted, not changed: "(Bertrand's postulate)" is presented as the proof method, but Bertrand is a consequence/companion, not the route to the bounds.
The product converges only for Re(s) > 1 overstated; Euler products also converge (conditionally) on Re(s) = 1. Changed to "converges absolutely only for Re(s) > 1".
Dropped qualifier: a^((p+1)/4) is a square root only when a is a residue (for a non-residue its square is −a). Added "and a a residue".
Clarity only: the step "6 − 4 = 2 lies in it" did not show why 6 is in p²; added that 6 is the difference of the last two generators.

Belief stated generally ("without unique factorization an element can factor into different numbers of irreducibles") is true in rings with class number >= 3, so the correction only refuted it for Z[sqrt(-5)]. Narrowed the belief to Z[sqrt(-5)] and made the Carlitz sentence say "a ring of integers ... its class number".

The product converges only for Re(s) > 1 overstated (the zeta Euler product also converges on Re(s) = 1, s != 1), and "the product formula does not apply there" is not a safe claim about the strip. Rewrote the correction: converges absolutely only for Re(s) > 1 with no zeros there; that says nothing about the continued function in the strip.

Correction (nine imaginary quadratic fields with h = 1) only refutes the belief for imaginary quadratic fields; for real quadratic fields h = 1 is conjectured common. Narrowed the belief to imaginary quadratic fields.
Core Idea credited the sum-of-two-squares theorem with characterizing which numbers need four squares; that is Legendre's three-square theorem. Fixed the name.
